newsitem.title: LEBANON: U.S. ban on Lebanon travel had looked dated.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ban on Lebanon travel had looked dated.

text.p: The U.S. ban on travel to Lebanon had come to look increasingly anachronistic as vast projects remade Beirut and foreign investors poured millions of dollars into a country labelled too dangerous to visit.

"The Americans are safe. They will be safe," Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri said after the United States formally ended the 12-year-old travel ban on Wednesday. "A lot of them came here before, during the years of the ban, and nothing happened to them."
In addition to tens of thousands of Americans who also held Lebanese passports, many other Americans have visited in recent years with Lebanese authorities obligingly not stamping their passports.

But the ban had limited foreign contacts. One official of a U.S. financial institution said in London he had been refused U.S. State Department permission to visit five times despite being active in Lebanese financial affairs.

The American University of Beirut (AUB), advertising for a new president, had to warn candidates the one chosen would actually run the Arab world's best known academic centre from the United States until the travel ban was lifted.

Although the return of normal life in Beirut has made Lebanese see the travel ban as increasingly political -- U.S. pressure for Lebanon to make peace with Israel -- there are ample historic reasons for U.S. nervousness.

When John Waterbury, named the new AUB president this month, eventually arrives he will take up residence on the campus where one of his predecessors in the 1980s was assassinated and a second was kidnapped.

The kidnapping of David Dodge, the AUB president in 1982 when Israel invaded Lebanon, was a sign of things to come. Although he was released on the first anniversary of his seizure, anti-U.S. sentiment was taking ever more deadly forms.

A suicide truck bomb attack in 1983 killed 241 U.S. servicemen, who were positioned around Beirut airport following the Israeli invasion. Two other suicide attacks killed dozens of American diplomats.

In March 1984 Islamic Jihad Moslem militants -- which the United States maintains is just a cover for the pro-Iranian Hizbollah movement -- kidnapped William Buckley. Buckley, who was reported tortured to death, was the station chief for the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency.

Most subsequent kidnappings had little to do with the victims' politics or occupations. Although French, German, British and other nationalities were among those seized, Americans appeared to be the prized captives.
A hijacking of a TWA airliner to Beirut in 1985, and the killing of a U.S. passenger, provided the trigger for the United States to formally ban its citizens from visiting Lebanon.

Even as U.S. officials struggled to free hostages, others -- including several on the staff of the AUB -- continued to disappear into Islamic Jihad dungeons. Only as the civil war drew to a bloody close in 1990, did the longest held Westerners begin to be released.

Terry Anderson, the Associated Press bureau chief who had been seized in March 1985, was finally freed on December 4, 1991 -- after 2,545 days of often brutal captivity. He was the last American hostage.

While diplomats of other countries have since returned to a near normal status in Beirut -- although they often have bodyguards nearby -- the United States continues to exercise extreme caution. U.S. diplomats normally travel in heavily armed convoys and the embassy is a fortress.
But other Americans had grown increasingly sceptical of the travel ban after years without a direct threat to U.S. citizens despite the continuing Middle East unrest.

"I think it's great and it's about time," U.S. citizen Nadine Alfa said after the ban was lifted. "We've lived here for so long and have American friends here. It's much safer than in New York or Boston."

Although U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said in lifting the restriction that Washington would continue to advise its citizens against any travel to Lebanon, even Anderson returned on the fifth anniversary of his release.

"Most people, Americans and others, have a really outdated and simplistic view of Lebanon" he said last December. "They think it's all war, kidnapping, bombs. That's not really what Lebanon is all about."
